bib.title: Agent Laboratory: Using LLM Agents as Research Assistants

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Agent Laboratory: Using LLM Agents as Research Assistants", Schmidgall, Su, Wang, Sun, Wu, Yu, Liu, Moor, Liu, Barsoum (AMD, JHU, ETH Zurich). Preprint, arXiv:2501.04227v2 [cs.HC], 17 Jun 2025.

COVERAGE: 84 of 84 pages; all 169,259 chars (count includes my page markers). Nothing skipped. References (pp. 22-30) were skimmed for origins. Prompts (pp. 32-56) and survey forms (pp. 57-84) were read. Pages 11, 13, 15, 17 and 18 were also rendered, because the result tables are images with no text layer.

CLAIMS (page = PDF page = printed page)

- claim: Average API inference cost per workflow is $2.33 on gpt-4o, $7.51 on o1-mini and $13.10 on o1-preview, and $2.33 is the gpt-4o figure only.
  number: $2.33 / $7.51 / $13.10
  setup: Seven subtasks from literature review to report refinement. The section does not state the mode or the run count. Table 1 settings: 3 mle-solver steps, 5 paper-solver steps, 600s experiment timeout. Run on a MacBook M3 Max (p. 31).
  quote: "Monetary costs per workflow were also substantially lower for gpt-4o, which averaged just $2.33 for the entire process." / "such as o1-mini at $7.51, and o1-preview at $13.10"
  where: p. 17
- claim: The 84% saving is a comparison with The AI Scientist's roughly $15, which is a different pipeline.
  number: ~$15, 6.4x, 84%
  setup: gpt-4o only. The $15 is taken from Lu et al., not rerun. The best-rated backend (o1-preview, $13.10) is only about 13% below $15 (my arithmetic).
  quote: "previous autonomous research workflows (Lu et al. (2024b)), which cost around∼$15 (6.4x more expensive)" / "achieving an 84% decrease compared to previous autonomous research methods"
  where: p. 17; p. 1
- claim: Report Writing is the most expensive phase across models.
  number: $1.73 / $2.58 / $9.58
  setup: gpt-4o / o1-mini / o1-preview. On o1-mini, Data Preparation ($3.03) is actually the top phase after Report Writing's $2.58, per Fig. 8, which contradicts "across models".
  quote: "its costs for Data Preparation and Report Writing were $0.09 and $1.73, respectively, compared to $3.03 and $2.58 for o1-mini, and $0.30 and $9.58 for o1-preview."
  where: p. 17
- claim: Automated reviewers rate the autonomous papers far above human reviewers do.
  number: 6.1/10 vs 3.8/10 (-2.3); clarity 3.6/4 vs 2.4/4
  setup: Same 15 autonomous papers. LLM reviewer adapted from Lu et al., against human PhD volunteers. Fig. 6 also shows the backend order inverting: automated gpt-4o 6.2 > o1-mini 6.0 > o1-preview 5.9; human 3.5 < 3.8 < 4.0 (image reading).
  quote: "While the automated reviewers gave an average overall above average NeurIPS paper score of 6.1/10, human reviewers provided a much lower average of 3.8/10 (-2.3 points)."
  where: pp. 12-14
- claim: Autonomous papers score below the average accepted NeurIPS 2024 paper.
  number: 3.5, 3.8, 4.0 by backend; 5.85 benchmark; -2.05
  setup: The benchmark comes from a papercopilot.com statistics footnote (p. 14). p. 12 rounds it to 5.9. Raters were not actual NeurIPS reviewing cohorts.
  quote: "average overall ratings ranging from 3.5/10 with gpt-4o, 3.8/10 with o1-mini, and 4.0/10 with o1-preview." / "NeurIPS 2024, which stands at 5.85∗ (our scores were -2.05 points lower on average)"
  where: pp. 12, 14
- claim: The first human evaluation used 10 volunteer PhD students rating 15 autonomous papers on a 1-5 scale.
  number: 15 papers, 10 raters, 3 papers each, scale 1-5
  setup: 5 ML/NLP/CV questions x 3 backends. This implies about 2 ratings per paper (my arithmetic). NeurIPS criteria use 1-4; overall uses 1-10.
  quote: "resulted in a total of 15 papers being written au-\ntonomouslyby Agent Laboratorywithoutanyhumaninvolvement. Wethenrecruited10volunteer\nPhD students to review 3 randomly assigned papers each."
  where: p. 11
- claim: On the 1-5 scale, usefulness rates much higher than experimental quality on every backend.
  number: gpt-4o 2.6 / 3.0 / 4.0; o1-mini 3.2 / 3.2 / 4.3; o1-preview 2.9 / 3.4 / 4.4 (experiment / report / usefulness)
  setup: Autonomous mode, the 5 preselected topics. Scores swing widely by topic (image noise on gpt-4o: 1.5/5 experiment).
  quote: "an average experimental quality rating of 2.6/5, a report quality rating of 3.0/5, and a usefulness rating of 4.0/5" / "with an average score of 3.2/5 (+0.6)" / "averaging 4.4/5" / "at 2.9/5 (+0.3 from gpt-4o and -0.3 from o1-mini)"
  where: p. 11
- claim: External evaluators rate co-pilot papers higher than autonomous ones, but still below the NeurIPS benchmark.
  number: 4.38 vs 3.8 (+0.58); -1.45 below 5.85
  setup: o1-mini for all phases except literature review. Two papers per researcher (custom and preselected). Number of researchers and external evaluators not stated. The autonomous baseline pools all three backends. Largest gains are in quality (+0.75) and soundness (+0.48); significance falls (-0.05).
  quote: "the largest improvements were seen for quality, which increased by +0.75, soundness, which improved by +0.48, and the overall score, which improved by +0.58." / "co-pilot overall scores, which average at 4.38, are still -1.45 points below the average score of 5.85"
  where: p. 16
- claim: Humans co-piloting rated the output lower than raters of autonomous o1-mini output did, on the same 1-5 items.
  number: experiment 2.38 (-0.82), report 3.13 (-0.07), usefulness 3.75 (-0.55)
  setup: Different people rating different papers. Authors attribute the drop to difficulty steering agents to a precise vision.
  quote: "While report quality was only rated -0.07 points lower, usefulness was rated -0.55 points lower and experiment quality was -0.82 points lower." / "the reduction in scores is due to difficulty guiding the agents to execute their exact vision for the project."
  where: p. 15
- claim: Human self-evaluation is lower than external evaluation, the opposite direction from the LLM gap.
  number: self 4.13/10 vs external 4.38/10 (+0.25); quality +0.62; clarity -0.25
  setup: Co-pilot papers. Self-raters prefer their custom topics (4.25 vs 4.0); externals prefer preselected (4.5 vs 4.25, Fig. 7).
  quote: "with an overall average of 4.38/10, up from 4.13/10 in self-evaluations. The most significant improvements were observed in quality (+0.62), significance (+0.25), and overall (+0.25) scores"
  where: p. 16
- claim: Tool ratings from co-pilot users are moderate to good.
  number: utility 3.5, continuation 3.75, satisfaction 3.63, usability 4.0 (/5); 75% answered the optional feedback question
  setup: Self-report after one session on each of two topics.
  quote: "the overall scores across all experiments are 3.5/5 for utility, 3.75/5 for continuation, 3.63/5 for satisfaction, and 4.0/5 for usability"
  where: p. 14
- claim: mle-solver earned the most medals on 10 low-complexity text and tabular MLE-Bench challenges.
  number: 4 medals (2 gold, 1 silver, 1 bronze) vs OpenHands 2, AIDE 2, MLAB 0; above human median 6/10, AIDE stated 5/10, OpenHands 2/10, MLAB 0/10
  setup: 10 of MLE-Bench's 75. Solver scored on a 20% dev split, not by the LLM reward model used in the full workflow, then evaluated on the Kaggle test set. Given distilled Kaggle-notebook knowledge. Comparators: MLAB and OpenHands on gpt-4o, AIDE on o1-preview. Invalid comparator submissions were excluded from their averages. mle-solver's backend and run count are not stated.
  quote: "withmle-solver obtaining four medals (two gold, one silver, and one bronze) compared with OpenHands (gpt-4o) obtaining two medals (two gold), AIDE (o1-preview) obtaining two medals (one gold, one bronze) and MLAB obtaining zero medals." / "obtained above median human performance on six out of ten benchmarks, with AIDE obtaining five out of ten, OpenHands two out of ten, and MLAB zero out of ten." / "Instead of using an LLM scoring function"
  where: pp. 18-19
- claim: The "entire workflow" success rate is a mean of subtask rates, not an end-to-end completion rate.
  number: 95.7% / 94.3% / 92.8%; literature review 60/70/80%
  setup: o1-preview / gpt-4o / o1-mini. Means reproduce from Fig. 8 (my arithmetic). Fig. 8 labels 60/70/80 as success; the text calls them failure.
  quote: "achieving the highest average subtask success rate (95.7%)" / "the literature review phase had a high rate of failure, at 60%, 70%, and 80% for gpt-4o, o1-mini, and o1-preview respectively."
  where: p. 18
- claim: gpt-4o is the fastest backend.
  number: 1165.4s; 3616.8s; 6201.3s
  setup: Whole workflow. Experiment execution dominates the o1 times.
  quote: "completing the entire workflow in 1165.4 seconds, approximately 3.2x faster than o1-mini and 5.3x faster than o1-preview, which required 3616.8 seconds and 6201.3 seconds"
  where: p. 17
- claim: Failure modes include repeated commands, token overruns, unfixed 0% accuracy, process-killing exit() calls, host system commands and fruitless arXiv searches.
  number: up to 100 search tries, later limited to 5
  setup: Observed during runtime; no frequencies given. exit() had to be removed manually. subprocess.run() was seen on the host: "safeguards should be implemented".
  quote: "it could take up to100 tries for a successful search query to return any papers. A limit of5 was place thereafter"
  where: p. 20
- claim: gpt-4o papers sometimes hallucinate experimental details.
  number: none as a rate (the quoted example invents lr 0.001, batch 32, 50 epochs)
  setup: Authors call it uncommon and worse in lower-performing models. No count given.
  quote: "there were hallucinations regarding experimental results that did not occur"
  where: p. 20
- claim: The Lu et al. reviewer's validation does not carry over to these generated papers.
  number: 65% vs 66% accuracy; F1 0.57 vs 0.49; agreement 53.3% vs 56.1%
  setup: First two pairs are on 500 ICLR 2022 papers. The third pair's source sentence is garbled and its citation unclear.
  quote: "the automated reviewer achieved human-level accuracy (65% compared to 66% for human reviewers) and surpassed human performance in F1 score (0.57 vs. 0.49)" / "with lower agreement scores (53.3% vs. 56.1%)"
  where: pp. 9, 19

LIMITS
Authors concede:
- Reports are "less satisfying" than The AI Scientist's and have lower-quality figures, despite higher automated scores (p. 19).
- Reports are not meant to replace human paper writing, yet NeurIPS scores are the quality heuristic (pp. 8, 19).
- Section structure is fixed, reports are capped at two figures, and there is no repository-level code management (pp. 19-20).
- Evaluations are "only a snapshot"; a longitudinal with/without study is left as future work (p. 22).
- Ethics section covers flooding peer review and misuse (pp. 20-21).

The paper does not show:
- Any significance test, confidence interval or standard deviation. A term search of pp. 1-31 finds none, and "correlat" returns no hits, so "not predictive" (p. 13) has no statistic behind it, and the abstract's "significantly improves" is untested.
- The number of co-pilot researchers or external evaluators. Quarter-point scores and the 75% response rate suggest 4 per condition, but that is my inference.
- Rater blinding: the form tells raters the report "was generated by an AI tool" and asks whether it is "useful for me to build off of instead comparing it to what a human would perform" (p. 57), which may inflate usefulness.
- Accept/reject decisions and confidence: the forms collect them (p. 64), but they are not reported.
- Co-pilot cost or time: runtime is reported by backend only, and co-pilot ran on o1-mini, so $2.33 is not a co-pilot figure. Human labour and failed-run cost are also not addressed; the price table is not given.
- Research novelty or replication: nobody checks whether the generated findings are correct. Topics are ML only.
- Ideation: the pipeline starts from a human idea (p. 1). This bears on target note line 411, which says it "covers the same span" as The AI Scientist "with human oversight, at $2.33".

Dated: gpt-4o, o1-mini and o1-preview backends; costs reflect prices at the time of the runs.

BUILDS ON:
- Lu et al. (2024b), The AI Scientist: reviewer prompt and section tips (pp. 9, 48, 50).
- Schmidt et al. (2024), AIDE: Solution Space Search (p. 7).
- Yao et al. (2024): tree search analogy (p. 7).
- Shinn et al. (2024) and Renze & Guven (2024): self-reflection (p. 7).
- Chan et al. (2024): MLE-Bench (p. 18).
- Huang et al. (2024): MLAB; Wang et al. (2024b): OpenHands (p. 19).
- Si et al. (2024): complementary role for LLMs (p. 2).

CODE (verbatim)
- Budget nudge, appended once steps reach 70% of the limit (p. 32): "You must finish this task and submit as soon as possible!"
- Anti-loop line in the base prompt (p. 32): "Your previous command was: {self.prev_comm}. Make sure your new\noutput is different."
- Guard in the mle-solver system prompt (p. 43): "Your method MUST not get 0% accuracy. If it does, you have done\nsomething wrong and must correct this."
- Section tip (p. 50): "Only includes results that have actually been run and saved in the\nlogs. Do not hallucinate results that don’t exist."
- Reward-model prompt (p. 42): "determine how well a model followed the plan, built the code,\nand got the proper output scored from 0 to 1 as a float."

FIGURES (values read from images, not in the text layer; re-check against the render before citing)
- Fig. 8, p. 17, "Performance and Cost Evaluation": fastest way to see where money goes. Cost by phase:
  - gpt-4o: lit .12, plan .03, data .09, experiments .18, interpretation .16, writing 1.73, refinement .02, total 2.33.
  - o1-mini: .16, .22, 3.03, 1.05, .40, 2.58, .07, total 7.51.
  - o1-preview: .31, .04, .30, 2.59, .21, 9.58, .09, total 13.1.
  - Costs sum correctly (my check).
  - Success: lit 60/70/80; data 100/80/90; all others 100.
- Fig. 6, p. 13, split violin and tables of automated vs human scores: shows the evaluation gap at a glance, and the best teaching candidate. By gpt-4o / o1-mini / o1-preview, on 4-point criteria:
  - Automated overall: 6.2 / 6.0 / 5.9.
  - Human quality 1.8 / 2.3 / 1.9; significance 2.2 / 2.2 / 2.5; clarity 2.6 / 2.1 / 2.4; soundness 1.8 / 1.7 / 2.2; presentation 2.7 / 2.4 / 2.4; contribution 1.9 / 2.2 / 2.3.
  - Human overall: 3.5 / 3.8 / 4.0.
- Fig. 7, p. 15, "Co-pilot evaluation": self, external and delta from autonomous in one table.
  - Self overall: preselected 4.0, custom 4.25.
  - External overall: preselected 4.5, custom 4.25.
  - Delta autonomous: +.75, -.05, +.23, +.48, +.33, +.03, +.58.
- Fig. 9, p. 18, MLE-Bench per-challenge table: shows the wins and the collapses together. mle-solver gold on detect insults (0.839) and dec 2021 (0.961), silver on predict conductors (0.062), bronze on english text (0.990). Failures: russian text normalization 0.000, NYC taxi 6.542 vs median 3.597.
- Fig. 5, p. 11: score by question and backend; shows topic variance.
- Fig. 2, p. 5: three-phase workflow with agents and tools.
- Fig. 3, p. 7: mle-solver loop.
- Fig. 4, p. 8: paper-solver.
- Fig. 1, p. 1: pipeline overview.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions aimed at me. The prompts on pp. 32-56 are the paper's own agent prompts, treated as data.
- `scripts/papers/figures.py captions` printed nothing, so captions and pages were taken from the text and renders. Renders are in /tmp/agentlab-pages/.
- Extraction drops spaces in places and the tables are images; quotes keep those faults, with \n marking line breaks.

Internal inconsistencies in the paper:
1. AIDE above-median: text says 5/10 (p. 19), but Fig. 9 shows 6 ticks, tying mle-solver. Checked on a 340-dpi crop.
2. Fig. 9 bolds mle-solver's 0.532 on spooky author, a Min task where AIDE's 0.320 is better. Corrected row by row, AIDE and mle-solver each lead 5 of 10 (my count).
3. Soundness: text gives "o1-mini and gpt-4o at 1.8 (-0.4) and 1.7" (p. 12); Fig. 6 shows gpt-4o 1.8, o1-mini 1.7.
4. p. 2 says o1-preview was best "particularly in clarity", but Fig. 6 has gpt-4o highest on human clarity (2.6 vs 2.4).
5. Image-noise usefulness with o1-mini: 4.5 in text (p. 12), 4.0 in Fig. 5.
6. Workflow times for gpt-4o and o1-preview do not sum: phases total 1181.9s and 6234.5s, against 1165.4s and 6201.3s. The stated totals match the sums without refinement. o1-mini sums correctly.
7. Presentation delta from autonomous: +0.33 in text and Fig. 7, but 2.88 - 2.5 = +0.38 (also for the self-evaluation).
8. Repair attempts: N_rep=3 on p. 6, 2 in Table 1 (p. 31).
9. p. 14 garbles the usability comparison: "lower across all measures... except for usability which was -0.5 points lower"; Fig. 7 has preselected higher on usability (4.25 vs 3.75).
10. Fig. 6's caption states the direction backwards ("Human scores are not predictive of automated reviewer scores"; p. 21 says the reverse).
